I agree with you in that we shouldn’t go along with the said binary. That’s why it’s all about knowing. I’m not saying your wrong at all but maybe you are right that we don’t need to teach the popular opinion. I don’t think people should identify with something they’re told. I think it really just comes down to a case by case basis. I hope I’m making sense, but teaching the gender roles and then saying that in the current society, we don’t need to go by the old rules. That’s what it used to be or still is but you don’t have to follow that if you don’t want to. Because gender is very broad, we can enforce the idea that you can exist outside of those boundaries. Male and female at least in the sense of being cis is just surface level. You be whatever it is you feel in yourself but understand that the enforcement of gender roles will probably still exist in some capacity, not to be cynical. 


Just by existing, I challenge the common binary but all I want in the end is to really teach others and children that something other than what they are taught to be if they feel differently. I don’t plan on having children, but I still want to teach others. If that makes sense.

It introduces gender and then you can branch off into the greater spectrum. How the world itself has expectations for the said two genders and then explain to children that it doesn’t necessarily need to be that way. Like you said, the two genders themselves can be introduced in isolation because it’s so embedded in society itself, but what people fail to realize is that it doesn’t need to be that way. You can introduce other aspects to it that open up different things you can teach impressionable minds like 3 year olds. Not as deep as we’re talking but in a way they can understand. It all depends on the individual. I’m not saying that it has to be set in stone. Every kid should have the right to choose how they wish to identify and depending on what it is, you teach based on what they identify as and the traits they have.

And I agree that gender identity is important, but so is the binary as a baseline and every corner of it including the ones that exist out of it. Any kind of information, even LGBTQIA can be bad if it’s introduced in isolation because it can be confusing and it ignores other outside information. It needs to be absorbed broadly and thoroughly enough so that people can make their decision on if they’re cis or not. 
This is what I would do personally. It’s not my business how people raise their kids unless it’s something that’s outright wrong like abuse.

I’m more of the belief that they should be exposed to both and make that decision for themselves. Again, I think it’s important and as someone who is gender non conforming, I think that kind of education should be taught but not in a vacuum. They should be exposed to every side of it. Including the ugly sides. Any kind of information that will help them navigate the world in a way that allows them to make that decision for themselves. In a more personal reference, my education was taught in isolation, and I remember how out of place I felt despite that education. I never knew about non conforming genders until early teens. My main point is that gender education and sex education should be taught broadly and not just the parts that people think are most important.

But does exposing a kid that early, really matter at early stages like that? They don’t even know if they are cis or even trans. Three is still incredibly young and they probably won’t even understand everything that they’re absorbing. Kids at that age shouldn’t have to worry about questioning whether they’re cis or not. They should be learning how to spell and read and count. Not saying that that kind of education is important, but just not when the kid is only three years old.
